The gestation period lasts approximately thirty days [tg = approximately thirty days], a duration that is consistently observed when females maintain a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Newborn pups emerge from the birth canal weighing an average of 10.5 grams [Wwb = 10.5 grams], with recorded values spanning from 8.1 to 13.2 grams depending on maternal condition and litter size. This neonatal mass is modest compared to the ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, which can reach up to 580 grams [Wwi = up to 580 grams] in prime individuals, although the typical range extends from 250 to 580 grams. The rapid growth trajectory from birth to this adult size requires substantial energetic investment during the early suckling period.

Following parturition, the altricial neonates remain entirely dependent on maternal milk during an extended nursing stage. This weaning age is somewhat longer than the gestation period itself, reflecting the considerable parental investment required to rear these pups to the point of dietary emancipation. The mother's metabolic rate must elevate substantially to support lactation, and this period represents the most energetically demanding phase of the annual cycle. The successful transition to independent feeding is a critical developmental milestone that precedes the juvenile stage, during which the young animals must accumulate sufficient body reserves to survive their first hibernation season.
